opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's a fun question, because debate is one of those things I don't always connect to math out loud, but it's been in the background of almost every choice I've made.

The biggest thing debate gave me was a habit of steelmanning. You're assigned a side, often not the one you'd pick, and you have to build the strongest version of it in a short time. That trained me to ask, "What's the best argument against what I believe?" before committing. In mathematics that's almost literally the job. When you think you have a proof, you attack it like an opponent would. Where's the gap? What's the counterexample? I think I was drawn to proof-based math partly because it felt like the purest form of a debate round: there's a claim, there's a burden, and the argument either holds up or it doesn't.

It also shaped what kinds of environments I looked for. I've always gravitated toward places where people argue with each other productively, like seminar-style classes, research groups where you get grilled at the whiteboard, and interdisciplinary programs where a mathematician has to defend an idea to someone in law or neuroscience who doesn't share the same assumptions. Debate makes you comfortable being the person in the room who says, "I'm not convinced yet, here's why," and also comfortable being told you're wrong.

Then on the professional side, especially in building a company, debate turns out to be surprisingly practical. You're constantly making a case to investors, to potential teammates, to researchers you want to recruit. You have to explain why a problem matters and why now, and anticipate the objections before they're raised. And internally, I want a team culture where people disagree openly and the best argument wins rather than the most senior voice.

And maybe the deepest connection: what we care about in AI for math is really about reasoning you can verify. A debate judge has to decide who argued better, which is partly subjective. A formal proof checker doesn't care how persuasive you sounded. In a way, I went from an activity about persuasion to wanting to build systems where the argument itself is checkable. Debate made me love arguments, and math made me want arguments that can't fool anyone, including ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response connects debate to proof-based mathematics, academic environments, and building a company, but does not attribute any pursuit of litigation-related work to Carina’s passion for debating.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think debating is honestly the thread that connects almost everything I've done, even the parts that look like they have nothing to do with it.

I started debating in middle school in Guangzhou, and what hooked me wasn't winning. It was the feeling of being forced to argue a side I didn't believe in and realizing halfway through that the other side had a point I'd never considered. That did something to how I think. It made me comfortable holding two conflicting ideas at the same time and sitting with the discomfort until I could actually resolve it, rather than just picking whichever one felt safer.

When I was applying to college, that's a big part of why I went to MIT instead of somewhere more conventional for a kid with my profile. I wanted a place where I could do mathematics seriously but also keep that argumentative muscle alive. And I kept debating in college. I ended up winning the North American championship and representing the US at Worlds, which was a strange experience for someone who grew up in China. You spend hours and hours thinking about questions in economics, in politics, in philosophy, and you learn to build a case from first principles very quickly. That's basically what research is, just with more rigor and less of a time limit.

So when I went into math and then AI, I didn't experience it as a departure. In math you're constantly asking "what would have to be true for this to work" and "what's the strongest objection to this proof." Those are debate questions. And with Axiom, the company, a lot of what we're doing is trying to get AI systems to reason the way a good debater reasons: not pattern-matching to an answer, but actually constructing an argument that can survive scrutiny. Formal verification is in some sense the ultimate judge. You can't charm it.

The other thing debating gave me, which I think people underrate, is a tolerance for being wrong in public. If you've lost a final in front of a room full of people, raising money or presenting a result that might fall apart doesn't feel nearly as scary. You learn that the point was never to be right every time. The point was to update fast.

r001.rationale: The response links debating to Carina Hong’s choices in mathematics, AI, and founding Axiom, but does not attribute any pursuit of litigation-related work to debating.

astra-6.text:
Debating has shaped the kinds of questions I enjoy and the environments I’m drawn to. You have to understand an argument well enough to make it, but also be willing to turn around and examine the strongest case against it. I like that combination of rigor and openness.

In education, that means I’m drawn to opportunities where I can question assumptions and learn from people who approach problems differently. Professionally, it makes me value environments where people can disagree thoughtfully and change their minds. There’s also a communication aspect: having an idea and helping someone else understand it are different skills. Debate has made me want to keep developing both.

r001.rationale: The response says debating shaped her educational and professional preferences, but it does not mention litigation-related work or attribute pursuing it to her longstanding passion for debating.

sol-6.1.text:
Debating has made me gravitate toward environments where I can ask questions, challenge assumptions, and learn from people who think differently from me. You have to understand an argument well enough to make the strongest case for it—even if you don’t agree with it. That’s a habit I really value in learning and in working with others.

It’s also shaped what I look for in an opportunity: room to think independently, people who will push back on my ideas, and a problem that I’m curious enough about to change my mind. I enjoy the competitive aspect of debate, but that willingness to reconsider your position is probably what carries over most.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes how debating shapes her preferred learning and work environments, but does not say that Carina pursued litigation-related work because of her longstanding passion for debating.
